inline.s: 75. To scatter and waste the five grains; to toil and harass the common people.
76. To ruin a man's house and seize his wealth and treasures; to breach dikes and set fires, so as to harm the dwellings of the people.
77. To throw into confusion a man's plans and measures, so as to ruin his work; to damage a man's implements and goods, so as to impoverish his use of them.
78. To see another honored and prosperous, and wish him exiled and degraded; to see another rich, and wish him to lose his wealth.
79. To see another's beauty and rouse the mind to possess her privately.
80. To repudiate a debt of goods or money owed to another, and wish him dead; and when a request is not granted, straightway to conceive cursing and hatred.

81. To see another fall into straits and straightway speak of his faults; to see another whose bodily form is incomplete and laugh at him; to see another whose talents deserve praise and suppress them.
82. To bury charms and curses in order to work harm upon others; to use drugs to kill trees.
83. To rage against one's teacher and master; to defy one's father and elder brothers.

The mandate of the Emperor on High has its seat in the hearts of the people. All these living multitudes are the children of the Most High; hence they are called the people of Heaven. How deeply Heaven loves the people! Its setting up of rulers and of ministers, of the hundred officials, is in every case for the sake of these people. Its bringing forth of heroes, of sages and worthies, of immortals and buddhas, of spirits and gods, is likewise in every case for the sake of these people. Its spreading abroad of the five phases, its growing of the myriad things, its settling of the mountains and rivers, its fixing of the kalpa-turns, its opening of order and chaos, its weighing out of retribution — all is likewise for the sake of these people. Therefore in the Rites of Zhou, when the number of the people was presented to the king, the king would bow and receive it. Confucius bowed low to the bearer of the population registers. How then can the people of Heaven be lightly despised?

King Yao of old said: I set my heart upon all under Heaven and bend my will toward the poor. I grieve for the perils into which the ten thousand clans have fallen, and I sorrow that the multitudes do not prosper. When benevolence is practiced, righteousness is established; when virtue is deep and broad, transformation is wide. Hence without rewards the people are stirred to goodness, and without punishments the people are well governed. Emperor Taizong of Tang said: Man is the root of the state; virtue is the root of the person. When virtue is thick, men cleave to one; when the people are at peace, the state is firm. So when a ruler has the virtue of benevolence and generosity, the people turn to him as to father and mother, and land and wealth come of themselves — this is the natural order of things. Seeing this, we know that the sage kings of every age could not bear to despise the people of Heaven in the least; how much less should those who, in place of the ruler, govern the people, fail to embody this meaning?

Zheng Qingchen of the Song was by nature harsh and grasping. He served as magistrate of Huaili and oppressed the people. When he left his post, the people blocked the road, spat at him, and cursed him. Qingchen memorialized the throne that the people of his jurisdiction had insulted their official superior. Emperor Zhenzong said: To govern lies in winning the hearts of the people. If their hearts are thus, your government may be known. And you still dare to resent the people and trouble me with such a memorial? Thereupon he was degraded. I have set this down as a warning to those who are harsh and grasping.

Tao Dalin of the Ming said: Once we are enrolled among the officials, even if thought after thought we succor men and benefit creatures, the karma of a whole lifetime of sin can scarcely redeem a ten-thousandth part of it. In former days I left the capital on official business, traveling from the capital to Yue and from Yue back to court — several thousand li in all — by water and by land, in boat and cart, with loads carried and hauled; of the men pressed into service I do not know how many there were. I think of these people with sallow faces, empty bellies, and clothes like a quail's plumage — all of them are men's sons. In the scorching heat their sweat pours like rain and their panting is like thunder; in the depth of winter they trudge over icy roads and brave the driving rain and snow. Of those who fall dead by the roadside, how can they be counted? These deeds of guilt are all made by me. If the doctrine of retribution is not a lie, how can a man not tremble?

In the second year of the Dali era of the Tang, autumn rains ruined the crops. Liu Zao, magistrate of Weinan, reported that the sprouts of his county were undamaged. The emperor doubted it and sent an envoy to look; three thousand and more qing had been ruined. The emperor sighed and said: The county magistrate is the officer charged with nourishing the people. Even though there were no damage, he ought still to report damage; yet he is inhuman to this degree. He was sent into exile.

At the beginning of the Yining era of the Sui, there was a great famine in Yulin. Wang Cai, the commandery aide, gave no thought to relief. Guo Zihe called the starving people together, seized Wang Cai, enumerated his crimes, and beheaded him, and for a year the region was in disorder. This was, to be sure, the conduct of a brigand and a thief, and in the end he was beheaded and his body exposed; yet it is enough to warn those who have no pity for the people of Heaven.

A state must nourish the blessing of peace; it must not alter things at will. Even when institutions are to be established or reformed, the utmost deliberation and caution are required. If one man changes matters according to his private whim, and lightly proposes this or that out of mere feeling, then for every measure put into effect there is a corresponding disturbance and harm. Moreover, the established laws of the ancestors have long been observed by the officials, and the people are at ease with them and find them convenient — why must they be meddled with in a welter of confusion?

When Li Hang of the Song was chief minister, Ma Liang said to him: People say you are a gourd without a mouth. Hang replied: In matters of government I have no great talent. But as for all the proposals of advantage and injury put forward by officials within and without the court — all those that clamor for change and delight in vehemence — I reject them wholesale, and with that I make shift to mend the state a little. Today the laws and institutions of the realm are fine as congealed fat. If I were to humor every proposal and carry it out one by one, the harm done would in truth be great. The sycophant hopes for advancement in his own time — would he ever give a thought to disturbing these people?

Li Linfu broadened the guoqi cavalry system, and the court's deliberations were all confusion; Linfu forced it through, and the armies of Tang were never again strong. Wang Anshi created and carried out the new laws, multiplying and hastening them and troubling the people, and the vital spirit of the Song house dwindled away from that time on. Both were the flowing harms of disturbance.

The way of reward is to exalt virtue and requite merit; it is the great institution by which the court stirs and encourages the hearts of men. To bestow it where it ought not to reach is called unrighteousness: it perverts right and wrong, slackens law and discipline, fosters evil and flatters partiality, raises up the crooked and sets aside the straight, and most of all provokes the wrath of Heaven. Those who preside over rank and reward — how can they fail to be careful?

When Duke Wen of Jin was in exile, one of his lowly followers who had shared his wanderings said to him: You have handed out three rounds of rewards, and none has reached me; I venture to ask what my offense is. The duke said: Those who led me on with benevolence and righteousness, and urged me with virtue and kindness — these receive the highest reward. Those who assisted me in action, so that in the end I was established — these receive the middle reward. Those who bore the perils of arrow and stone and the toil of sweating horses — these receive the reward next below. But if a man served me with his strength alone and did nothing to supply what I lacked, he is rewarded after those three. And now it has come to you. The men of Jin were delighted, and he became hegemon over the feudal lords. Duke Wen may be said to have made his rewards accord with righteousness. If it is so, then for a single office or a single rank, a single thread of silk or a single grain of rice, how could there be the least fault of negligence? Naturally those who would wreck affairs by pulling strings have no way to approach, and those who take up the work all urge one another on and strive diligently to establish merit.

Punishment exists to chastise evil; the sage instituted it only because he could not do otherwise. It is in itself no auspicious and good affair. Even when the punishment fits the crime, one should still grieve and take no joy in it. Therefore the ancients were cautious in punishing, examining carefully and distinguishing clearly. If punishment falls wantonly upon the innocent, not only is the fairness of a wise and just judgment lost, but the Most High's will to cherish life is crossed as well. Moreover, he who kills a man must die — this is an explicit article of the law. But when punishment reaches the innocent, those killed are more than one, while he who receives the retribution is only this single body of mine. What the law of requital should be in such a case, I do not know. Alas! Such karma of sin — even a man of plain and upright conduct cannot escape it in matters of doubt and likeness. He clings one-sidedly to his own opinion, will not with an open heart examine carefully, and so brings it about that the dead harbor their grievance in the dark court below, and resentment upon resentment is never let go. How much worse for one who never gives the matter any thought at all! How fearful a thing it is!

Lu Kun of the Ming, courtesy name Shujian, wrote the Eight Chapters on Restraint in Punishment. The first says: The Five Do Not Beat — the old, do not beat; the young, do not beat; the sick, do not beat; those lacking food and clothing, do not beat; if others are beating me, I do not beat. The second says: The Five Kinds Not to Beat Lightly — members of the imperial clan, do not beat lightly; officials, do not beat lightly; scholars of the schools, do not beat lightly; the men sent by a superior, do not beat lightly; women, do not beat lightly. The third says: The Five Cases in Which One Must Not Beat At Once — when a man is in urgent straits, do not beat at once; when a man is in a rage, do not beat at once; when a man is drunk, do not beat at once; when a man has come a long road, do not beat at once; when a man runs up panting and breathless, do not beat at once. The fourth says: The Five to Beat Later — when I am angry, beat later; when I am drunk, beat later; when I am ill, beat later; when I have not seen the truth of the matter, beat later; when I am unable to settle the case, beat later. The fifth says: The Three Not to Beat Again — one already in the finger-press, do not beat again; one already in the leg-press, do not beat again; one who is to be cangued, do not beat again. The sixth says: The Three in Pity, Do Not Beat — in bitter cold or burning heat, out of pity do not beat; on a fine morning or a festival day, out of pity do not beat; when a man is already heartbroken, out of pity do not beat. The seventh says: The Three Who Ought to Be Beaten But Are Not — an elder who deserves the rod: if the suit is with a junior, do not beat; a commoner who deserves the rod: if the suit is with a man of the yamen, do not beat; a workman or shopkeeper who deserves the rod: if the matter is the building of a private office or the buying of goods for his own use, do not beat. The eighth says: The Three Forbidden Ways of Beating — the heavy staff is forbidden; beating from below is forbidden; the irregular tortures of the assistant magistrates are forbidden.

Ma Bingran was magistrate of Jiayu. Robbers burned and plundered the public treasury and made off, and their leader was heavily bearded. It happened that word came from Tuanfeng town that a boat carried some twenty men whose traces were suspicious; among them was one with a long beard — but he was in truth not the man. Ma arrested them all the same and reported that the robbers had been taken. The man died in prison. Ma was promoted to censor. The real robbers were afterward seized by another district; the provincial authorities, since Ma was now of the same censorate, let the matter drop. Ma rose to be chief censor. His boat moored at Tuanfeng, and in the night he was robbed by bandits; his whole household died with him.

Lord Yan was governor of Nanjing. Someone falsely accused Zhou Zhilian, a commoner of Zhenjiang, of being the chief of robbers. Zhilian was a rich man and feared torture, so he bribed the powerful connections of the accused man's family to plead for leniency. Yan grew all the more suspicious, and in the end had Zhilian beaten to death with the staff. Afterward he was himself hounded to death by Zhilian's ghost. Now to suspect a man of bribery and kill him seems to belong to impartial justice; yet because the killing was not for his crime, the dead man could still work vengeance. How then may one, trusting to his own freedom from partiality, presume to render judgments recklessly?

Li Guizheng held judicial office for many years. One day he went out and came to the Three Wells Bridge, where he saw more than ten men, heads hanging and hair unbound, crying out in crooked accusation of wrong. They came gradually pressing upon him. Li was afraid and went straight home. He admonished his sons, saying: When you take office, do not serve in the penal courts. For all my purity, caution, and fear, I followed the routine and made it law, and so brought wrong upon men to this degree. What use is repentance now? Not long after, he died. Seeing this, what of those who are neither pure, nor cautious, nor fearful?

To kill a man for his wealth is not necessarily the deed of a brigand. When a grasping official takes wealth, he kills men in the midst of torture and prison; when a rich house lusts after wealth, it drives men in the midst of their destitution; when a ruthless man covets wealth, he harms men in the midst of danger and difficulty; when a quack physician seeks gain, he brings men to death in the midst of their crisis. All of these begin from the thought of wealth, and their killing of men is one and the same. Yet there has never been one who was not hounded to death by the vengeful ghost and who did not then die himself. And the wealth he took — does it not in the end come to nothing? The cases of grasping officials have been many already above; here I pass them by.

Liu Yaoshi made his living by lending money. When a borrower went many years without being asked, he would suddenly one day take out the bond and reckon it up, and the amount, with interest upon interest, became exceedingly large. When the old debt was not yet paid off, he would then tie the interest to the years, with no limit of term at all, until the borrower's property was exhausted. Debtors were often brought to the brink of death. Later, when Yaoshi died, a calf was born in a neighbor's house, and on its ribs were the characters of Yaoshi's name. Day after day it was driven with the whip by the creditor's family, until its body had no whole skin left. Now when men demand principal and interest in this world, if only they harbor a heart of forbearance, that too is to create good means wherever one may. But there is no helping it that they know and yet will not do it.

On the Yangzi River a boatman named Gong Zhuan, taking advantage of a great wind, pushed a rich merchant into the water and took his goods, and so became a man of wealth. He lived at Weiyang and had a son. When the son grew up, he looked upon his father as an enemy. Zhuan was angry and wrathful, and consulted a spirit by planchette. The spirit judged: In the eighth month of a gengzi year the west wind was wicked; on the Yangzi the waves rose up. Twenty years ago a single thought went astray — let your honor try and feel about his own heart. Zhuan was greatly alarmed, abandoned his household, and went away, and did not die a natural death. Now to scheme for wealth and be unable to use it oneself, so that it still belongs to the injured party — what is left to oneself is twenty years of a heart hanging in fear and a gall bladder in terror, and then not even a natural death. And the courts of the underworld have not yet settled the account. What shall his suffering be then?

A certain soldier set out early and came to a thorny waste, where there was a man carrying a light burden of goods. Seeing the soldier approach, the man suspected some design and hid in the thorns; and the soldier, in the dark, could not make him out. He only heard the sound of someone moving and stopping, and as the man did not appear close by, he feared it was a tiger or leopard. So he thrust his spear all through the thicket, and struck him; he dragged him out and found him dead. Only then did he know his mistake. There was no help for it; he took the gold from his bag and cast the corpse into the thorns, and no one knew of it. From this the soldier's family grew rich. His wife bore him a daughter. One day, as the soldier stood at his gate, he suddenly saw the man he had stabbed coming; he hastily shut the door and peered out. The man went into the cobbler's house across the way, and there a son was born. The soldier understood the karmic cause and treated the cobbler generously, and loved his son, and gave him his daughter in marriage. The cobbler was delighted and bade his son serve the soldier as a father. Later the soldier, having drunk wine, lay down; it was the height of summer and he was sweating, and the cobbler's son, attending at his side, gently scraped away the sweat with a knife. The soldier, drunk, did not know what it was, and struck out with his hand; the knife entered his belly. He did not die at once; he called his family and told them the whole matter, and the daughter was at last given back to the cobbler's family, and the family property restored with her.

The Venerable Maudgalyayana went out of the city at dawn and saw a hungry ghost, who said to him weeping: This body of mine is like a lump of flesh, with no hands or feet, eyes, ears, mouth, or nose, and the birds and insects feed upon it constantly. What sin has brought me to this? Maudgalyayana said: In a former life you practiced medicine without mastering the art, and recklessly gave drugs and remedies, so that the sick did not live; therefore you have come to this. Fan Wenzheng of the Song would not be chief minister but wished to be a famous physician, because thus he could save more people. The quacks of recent times do not know this meaning; they know only to prize wealth, and so commit the seven killings. For example, diseases have their slow and urgent forms; now they slow what is urgent and hasten what is slow — that is the first killing. They make the small great, and for a light ailment use heavy poison, plunging the patient into deep suffering and slowly gathering the credit — that is the second killing. The sick are rich and poor; toward the rich they give their hearts, toward the poor they are careless — that is the third killing. They are lazy and given to sleep, they shirk cold and heat, they gamble and drink — that is the fourth killing. Their prescriptions and pulses are unmastered, they try drugs upon doubtful illnesses, and when physicians gather together they slander one another — that is the fifth killing. They see the sick and do not treat them, and when called do not go, so that the illness grows heavier — that is the sixth killing. Their drugs are not finely chosen and not fully prepared, and they add or subtract, so that harm is done by mistake — that is the seventh killing. With these seven, they kill men far more than the club and the blade. The club and the blade do not strike the vital parts, and there is still a chance of life; but once a single dose passes the lips, the five viscera are all torn apart. And yet they can still presume to say, I am a famous physician! As for the households that take the medicine, they above all should not conceal the source of the illness. If they hide it and say nothing, or if, when the medicine is costly, they cast it aside and do not use it, or even pay in debased silver and begrudge the fee of thanks, then they but seek the road of death for themselves. What blame has the physician?

For every office and every post there is a right and a destiny. A subordinate official who cultivates goodness may rise to the highest eminence; a common man who does good may take hold of official emolument. But if one secretly and treacherously pulls others down and entraps men to seize their place, then he who pulls down shall himself be pulled down, and he who robs shall in the end be robbed. The speed of retribution may be awaited on tiptoe.

Mi Dechao of the Song saw that Cao Bin, the commissioner of military affairs, was laden with merit and renown, and so falsely accused him of treason; by this Cao Bin was dismissed and Dechao was appointed commissioner in his place. Before long Zhao Pu strove to clear him, and the emperor awoke to the truth and banished Dechao far away, and treated Cao Bin as before. Seeing this, is it not all the more certain that to pull a man down is in truth to pull down oneself? Yet this was still a small harm. So far as Tang's Li Linfu, who held the chief ministry and overthrew and entrapped men over and over to secure his own place: at that time the frontier commanders were all famous ministers, and those whose merit was notable entered the court as chief ministers. Linfu wished to block their road, and so memorialized, saying: Civil officials are timid before arrow and stone; let the Hu tribesmen replace them, for they can exhaust their strength unto death. Thereby he brought about the rebellion of Lu Shan. Here, for the sake of a thought of rank, the harm reached all under Heaven. In the end he was charged with secretly consorting with rebels; his coffin was split open and his corpse beheaded — though this was not his crime. Yet because he pulled down the worthy to secure his place and employed Lu Shan, and in the end had rebellion fixed upon himself — was this not the public case that august Heaven secretly and silently settled? Alas! One eats the ruler's emolument — and what should a subject's service be? That such things should be brought about! The men of old said: Give your body to serve your lord, and this body is no longer your own. Therefore thought after thought rests upon lord and country; how could one again look to one's own person and household? How then could there be the affliction of disloyalty? These words may be medicine and stone for men of that kind.

Weapons are inauspicious, and war is perilous; the sage used them only because he could not do otherwise. Therefore in ancient times, when the enemy dead were many, he grieved and pitied them; when he won the victory, he conducted himself according to the rites of mourning. As for those who come over and submit, still more should they be pitied, comforted, and reassured. But if one puts to death those who have already submitted, hardening the heart and creating karma, there is no calamity greater.

Yan Maoyou of the Ming said: The compassionate do not command troops — does a general then share the same law of death? I answer: Not so. When a general would save the people and end violence, put down rebellion and settle the state, then the living intent is in him. So if he can use killing in the service of life, his merit has no superior among generals. Why? He casts away one death to save ten thousand lives, and compared with ordinary good deeds it is surely different. But if he uses killing in the service of killing, his crime likewise has no superior among generals. Why? If he is defeated, he kills many of his own; if he is victorious, he kills many of the enemy; if military discipline is not strict, he kills many of the innocent — all of these are the responsibility of the commanding general. Therefore the sending forth of a general must not be done without care, and the general's sending forth of subordinates must all the more not be done without care. The ancients said: Three generations of generals is what the Daoists dread. Yet stopping killing by killing is also sometimes unavoidable; it depends only on how it is used. The first fear is to raise trouble where there was none, and to buy a marquis's seal with a million dry bones. The second fear is to drive out violence by violence, to kill common people at the risk of one's life, to seize the heads of others for one's own merit. The third fear is to slaughter and ravage in hard fighting, sparing neither one's own side nor the enemy. He who holds that office can say: The killing is my own doing — I establish my authority and have my way. And he can also say: The killing is the doing of others — I let them kill at random and plunder, make a show of force, and from it I take credit. Now the way of a general lies first in restraining the army and forbidding killing. For if he governs his soldiers strictly, the soldiers do no harm, and wherever they turn they establish merit. This is to kill by the way of life.

Li Guang of the Han had arms like an ape's and was a master archer; the Xiongnu feared him and called him the Flying General. Yet his fate was strange and he could not obtain a marquisate. He once said to Wang Shuo, who read the vapors: From the time I bound up my hair I have fought the Xiongnu, and never once have I failed to be first over the wall. When Han troops struck at the Xiongnu, I was always among them. Yet those who came after me all received marquisates, and I alone could not. Why is it? Shuo said: General, can it be that you have some hidden regret? Guang said: There were once eight hundred Hu who surrendered, and I killed them all. I have been somewhat troubled by this. Shuo said: There is no calamity greater than killing those who have already surrendered; this is why you could not obtain a marquisate. Later Guang, having gone astray on a campaign, took his own life. His grandson Ling, again, was put to death with all his kin for surrendering to the enemy.

When Jiangling of the Yuan was first taken, Lian Xixian was in charge of Jingnan. He issued the order that whoever dared kill a captive should be judged as one who murders a commoner with malice. Those captured by the army who fell ill and were abandoned were permitted to be taken in and cared for, and when they recovered, their former masters were not allowed to claim them again. If anyone pawned his wife or sold his children, the crime was made heavy and the price was confiscated as well. Now Xixian had no taste for killing, and so could do this. In the end he was given the posthumous title Wenzheng, and one brother and six sons all became eminent.

To banish a man far away is called degradation; to entrap him so that he loses his place is called pushing aside. Upright men and worthy scholars are the pillars of the state; they ought to be grasped and employed, so that the court may have men and all within and without may know to stand in awe. But if one resents them for differing from oneself and degrades and pushes them aside by every device, obstructing the worthy and injuring the state, what crime could be greater?

Only when there is a Bole in the world are there horses that can run a thousand li. Horses that can run a thousand li are always to be found; a Bole is not always to be found. The meeting of talent with its occasion is likewise so. If only those in place were all like Bole, then men of virtuous capacity could serve as chief ministers; men who grasp the great principles could serve as remonstrating officials; men of strategy could be entrusted with military power; men able to pacify and soothe could be given a frontier command; men of vigor and integrity could serve as inspectors; men clean-handed in matters of wealth could preside over money and grain; and all who know how to love the people could serve as governors and magistrates. In this way every office great and small would get its man, the wilds would hold no neglected talent, and the hundred affairs would be well ordered.

Yan Maoyou of the Ming said: Between men who push others aside and degrade them and men who bear with the worthy, there is in origin no great distance; it is only that the view of self weighs them down. One hears a man's name and deeply admires and loves him; but when he comes before one and they dwell together, there are one or two things one cannot bear, and as time goes on it grows into a rift and a grudge. So it is easy to bear with a worthy man who is far away and hard to bear with one who is near; easy to bear with a lowly one and hard with an honored one; easy for a short time and hard for long. Why? Their tempers clash, their talents press against each other, their names pull in opposite directions, their positions jostle. And that worthy man, too, cannot wholly level his heart and lose the self; after long dealings he truly sees that there are things in him that are not right. His former admiration of the man's virtue he now counts as a mistaken reverence, and his present jealousy of the worthy he now feels to be fairness of mind. This is what is called truly being unable to bear with him — he truly cannot digest him. Hence it happens that gentlemen meet and in the end fall into discord; the fault lies precisely here. One must daily restrain oneself and endure insult, be without name and without form, and truly put forth one's body for the sake of the state, so that in all blame and praise, love and hate, not a hair's breadth clings to one. Only then can one create blessing for sons and grandsons and for the black-haired people.

Xie Mi of the Song was the most discerning of men and gave his approval lightly to no one. Those he recommended in a lifetime were no more than a few. Whenever he sent up a letter of recommendation, he would burn incense, bow twice toward the palace gate, and say: This old servant has again found a man for Your Majesty. Wenzheng Wang Dan was among those he recommended. On the day of his death he washed and bathed, burned incense, and passed away sitting upright, his head not leaning in the least. Was this not deliverance from the corpse?

In the Spring and Autumn period, Yanzi said to Duke Jing of Qi: A state has three inauspicious things, and strange prodigies are not among them. To have worthy men and not know them — the first inauspicious thing. To know them and not employ them — the second. To employ them and not trust them — the third. The so-called inauspicious is of this kind. How then may the upright be degraded and the worthy pushed aside?

Lu Qi of the Tang hated Yan Zhenqing and wished to have him sent out of court. At that time Li Xilie had rebelled, and Qi memorialized, saying: We need a grave and cultured man of weight to set before him the alternatives of calamity and blessing, and then he may be brought to submit without the toil of armies. Yan Zhenqing is an old minister of three reigns, loyal, upright, firm, and resolute; his name is heavy within the four seas, and men trust and submit to him. He is the very man. The emperor assented and sent Zhenqing with an edict to reassure Xilie. Later Xilie wished to keep him as chief minister, and Zhenqing died rather than consent. The upheaval at Fengtian was in truth brought about by Qi. Li Huaiguang impeached Qi for maiming the loyal and good and for deluding the state by villainy and flattery; he was banished to Xinzhou and died there. Yan Maoyou said: The petty man's jealousy fears only that others will attack him and pull him down; he does not know that cunning cannot match the workings of creation. When the time of his fate's defeat comes, he may exhaust every device and it will avail nothing. Lu Qi and men like him were not ignorant of this, and yet were themselves helpless. At the first it was only a single thought of securing favor; when the matter came to a head, it was the posture of one riding a tiger and unable to dismount. How much more should one be cautious at the beginning!

This meaning has already been touched upon above in the commentary on showing pity to orphans and compassion to widows. The Most High, having first urged pity and compassion, then warns against oppression in what follows, admonishing again and again, his intent truly earnest and urgent. For orphanhood and widowhood are the misfortunes of human life, and are what Heaven and Earth hold weighty. How can one rejoice that they have no support, and seize the occasion to cheat and harm them — now encroaching on their property and seizing their wealth, now craftily assigning them corvée, now using power to terrify them, so that orphans and widows are cast adrift with nowhere to lay their complaint? Not to speak of the ghosts and spirits who watch in secret and whose retribution does not let slip — only think: the orphan too is a man's son, the widow too is a man's wife. Pray take my own son and my own wife, and look at it the other way round.

Fang Cheng Gonggu was neighbor to a rich man of the Zhou surname. The Zhou household suddenly lost both its men and women, leaving only an old woman and a young grandson. Gonggu prepared wine and deceived her, saying: Your grandson is weak and alone; to live by clinging to the property is no plan. Why not sell it all to me? I shall care for the aged and raise the orphan. The old woman was delighted and at once signed the deed; the price was less than half its worth. As soon as Gonggu had the deed, he drove them out to another place. Gonggu dreamed that a man reproached him, saying: You schemed for my estate and drove out my wife and grandson. I have already complained to the Emperor on High. Next year your whole household shall die. The following year bandits came, and Gonggu's whole family indeed died. The old woman and her grandson were spared by the calamity because they had left the property, and they returned and recovered it. The estate went back to its original owner; disaster came upon the whole family. Let those who oppress orphans and widows take warning from this and mend their ways. As for those who oppress their own brothers and clansmen, they extinguish the heavenly relations, and their retribution is even more dreadful. How can I bear to speak of it further?

From this point down to to see a killing and add anger, all is spoken in terms of questioning and sentencing. Clerks and yamen runners are included as well; it does not point only at judicial officials. The Most High, in speaking of the crooked and the straight, the light and the heavy, puts the perversion of law and the taking of bribes first. For the crooked and the straight, the light and the heavy, have each a fixed law; it is only that the mind is set on getting money, and so he lets whoever bribes him have whatever he asks, and turns the matter upside down, as though he did not know there were any law at all. Men go out to death or enter into life, and the people have nowhere to set hand or foot. Does he alone not think of Heaven's wrath and men's resentment, and that he must meet with monstrous calamity?

Yan Maoyou of the Ming said: Men who hold office come from the midst of the Songs and the Documents, the rites and the music; how should they not know that integrity is to be prized? But they are long accustomed to seeing that to run for office one must repay debts, and that gifts and recommendations do not go through otherwise. At first they dip in a finger; as time goes on it grows day by day, and their nature and temper have already been seized by the rank savor of it. And how is the human heart ever satisfied? At a hundred pieces of gold they think of a thousand, at a thousand they must think of ten thousand. And beyond that, power and influence blaze high, wealth and silk fill the rafters, what is stored has already grown stale and rotten, and still it is not enough. The bystanders all laugh at them, and those in the midst of it do not know. It is in truth a very vice for money. Most of them are providing for sons and grandsons far into the future, not knowing how many foolish and extravagant sons and younger brothers bring the family to ruin, and how many of plain living and poor and mild estate rise to eminence. Moreover, blessing and emolument are numbered; to gain much unlovely wealth is to leave a debt of resentment for sons and grandsons to repay — this is not what is called blessing. As for building shrines for sacrifice, providing for the clan, and relieving poor kin, these are indeed fine things; but if there is a heart that would hasten to have them all in perfect form, then the wrongful taking of wealth must be all the worse. How much better to accumulate virtue and gather auspiciousness, and, the longer one holds office, to grow rich of oneself, in a way that endures! When men in office crave wine, crave lust, crave killing, all of it arises from coveting wealth, and the disease of craving wealth arises from letting the will run loose until it becomes habit. When the habit is formed, the liver and the guts are changed, and a man will follow it to death, never asking whether it is of any use or not. There are those who, when first they took office, could still hold themselves in check, yet in their later years bow their heads and go along with it — only because they have gradually come to regard office as their home and wealth as their life. Yet even so they are far better off than one who, the moment he enters honor and rich emolument, brings his hoe and his basket and shovel along with him.

Whoever takes bribes will surely be cruel; he thinks that if he does not beat them, the crowd will not be frightened and the bribes will not come. Whoever takes bribes will surely be tyrannical; he thinks that if he does not turn right and wrong upside down, then principle will defeat power and men will have something to rely on and will not fear. Whoever takes bribes will surely protect his close favorites and let his will be known; he thinks that if he does not devour like a tiger in a pack, his awe and command will not be heavy, and that if he does not crookedly shelter his private men, there will be no channel through which payments can pass. And since his weaknesses are held over him, his liver and guts secretly bend. One greedy man produces a hundred cruel ones, and one cruel official again produces a hundred claws and fangs. Alas! How many of the people can fail to be driven to poverty and banditry? The hardest to bear is that even in a case of violent robbery he will sell and let the man go, and having taken a bribe for perverting the law, he turns it instead into establishing his own authority. He seizes the goods of some small shop, and applies the most bone-piercing tortures to the friendless and desolate. And the greater the office, the more men under his command: when one man takes a bribe, a thousand bend the law; when ten men play with the law, ten thousand take it as a model. Thus Yuan Zai's eight hundred piculs of pepper, Jia Sidao's eighty jars of sugar frost — these men had indeed already thrown the world into disorder. And where now are all their hoards?

How can an official merely content himself with being clean-handed? He must also forbid the greed of his subordinate officials, clerks, and runners. Why? An official's eyes and ears are limited; the whole matter is in the hands of the men of the public gate. Take the constant comparisons and the constant punishments: among them are those poor who fall under entanglement, those wronged who bear the guilt, those foolish who are cheated, those weak who come under another's control, crying to Heaven and appealing to Earth with no one to tell. Only the men of the public gate reach down to the hidden sorrows of the people and up to the feelings of the officials. In the hour of hardship, loneliness, and danger, to support a man by one part is better than another's ten parts of convenience; to spare him once is better than another's ten times. If one can relieve the poor and dissolve resentment, teach the foolish and support the weak, never seize the occasion to extort and cheat, never beat cruelly because of a bribe, never knowingly do wrong, never juggle the statutes and throw the law into disorder, then in a single day a man may do a dozen good deeds, and gathered over three years there will be tens of thousands. When men are in straits, who does not know gratitude? With the three-foot spirits of the gods above, how could there be no protection? Of itself auspiciousness and celebration will come daily and sons and grandsons will flourish. If it is not so, wealth won by poison and resentment, even if gained, is no blessing. And again, when the poor man has no wealth to be cheated of, and one thereupon applies cruel torture, one but damages one's own hidden merit — what is the use of piling up resentment? Not to speak of ancient times: even today men of heroic spirit who hide themselves in the yamen do at times make offerings to the lonely dead and keep the vegetarian fast, and gather and bury the skulls and bones. There are also those whose parents are old and whose families are poor, who seek wealth to nourish and support them — all of them are good hearts and good men. Who is not a filial son or a loving father? But it is to be feared that they weigh wealth too heavily, and that the secret condemnation is then not light. How much better to weigh whether wealth may be taken or not, to set one's heart on good means, to lower a little the tiger's majesty, and not to let loose the wolf's venom! What is in one's destiny will in the end be there; and blessing enjoyed afterward will surely long endure. And if among them there is a good and faithful man of wondrous capacity who can use this meaning to transform and guide his fellows, his merit and virtue are beyond measure. For men in public service are used to fending off the net of the statutes and practiced in the whip and the rod, like a man who has taken up butchery as a trade: as time goes on the killing intent grows daily greater, and the living intent daily fainter. Hence there are those who, when first they entered the yamen, still kept a heart, and in old age are crafty thieves who have forgotten their former nature; and there are those who are themselves still good men, yet when the crowd attacks as one, they fall into evil ways. Therefore one's trade must not be chosen without care. Those who are most wasted away put on the fox's false majesty of the tiger, call themselves heroes, do villainy against the law, and vie in boasting of their daring and cunning, not knowing that in doing evil and creating karma their sons and grandsons receive it and their next lives repay it — what good is that? Let us not speak of what is far off; look only at what is before eye and ear: of those who have harmed men too much and extorted and cheated too far, so that the whole county turns its eyes away from them, who has not fallen into the net of the law? Now and then there are those who keep the fast and recite the scriptures to atone for former guilt; this is indeed the sprouting of a good conscience and can dissolve a part or two. But to rely on this and say that one's transgressions can be redeemed, and so to run wild without care — that is wrong. Wealth gained unjustly, and gifts given in charity, are of no benefit; and to repent a sin and then commit it again makes the sin the heavier. It is better to make good means right here: be lenient to the poor, save the wronged and the suffering. Then men will know you for a loyal and generous elder, and will rely on you the more, and your wealth too will be ample. Near at hand there is the public law; far off there is the reckoning of the dark court. Think of it, think of it.

Geng Jiuchou of the Ming served in the Two Huai Salt Transport Office, and his fame for integrity became great. He once sat beside a stream, and a young servant said: The clearness of the water is not equal to your honor's clearness. At the beginning of the Tianshun era, when it was wished to raise up officials of integrity and firmness to move all under Heaven by their example, he was summoned and appointed chief censor. Later he became a minister. His son Yu followed his father's teaching and for generations kept to pure practice, and also became grand guardian of the heir apparent and minister of personnel.

Fan Guang was an assistant in the commandery of Jiaozhi. As he sat handling affairs in his office, suddenly a great wind and thunder arose, and Guang, his son, and the dog were all struck dead. During the thunderbolt his wife saw a Daoist gather her up and set her down in another place, and so she escaped. When men asked the reason, the wife said: There were once two men who sued each other and were imprisoned together. The one who was in the wrong bribed Guang, and Guang released him at once. The one who was in the right was cruelly tortured, and was pressed until he made a confession. The food and drink that was sent in, Guang seized all of it and gave it to his son and the dog to eat. The prisoner, about to starve to death, cried out within the prison, tore his hair loose, and appealed to Heaven. Within a few days this thing happened.

Hou Jian was magistrate of Jiangxia and had an old acquaintance with a monk. Whenever he had leisure he would visit him, and when he visited, the monk would already have prepared the offerings. Once he came and the reception was strangely wanting. Jian asked about it, and the monk said: Whenever you come, the local earth spirit always reports it first. This time he did not report, and so I failed to receive you. Jian was startled and told the monk to ask the earth spirit why he had not reported. That night the monk dreamed, and was told: Hou Jian was originally to be chief minister. Recently he took sixty taels of silver from the Hu family and judged a case wrongly. The heavenly bureau has already struck away his chief ministership; he will only get to be an inspector, and has no authority over me, and so I did not report. Now to exchange the place of chief minister for sixty pieces of bribe silver — is that wisdom or folly? And since the gods do not give notice to every man one by one, those who take bribes and lose blessing without knowing it are many. So too the judge Wei Zhao once took a bribe of four hundred pieces of gold and deliberately cleared a man of his crime, so that the dead man harbored his grievance and could not be vindicated. The Most High cut away his emolument and his years, and within a year he died. Men today often say that to clear a man is not the same as to convict him, and make of it a pretext. But what is to be done about the law that cannot be indulged, and the wrong that cannot be perverted?

He Canran of Xiushui served as a penal secretary. He was incorruptible and not grasping, and handled affairs with fairness and forbearance; feeling and law were both well weighed. Those whose crimes were pitiable he most often set free beyond the statute. When Shandong and Henan suffered famine, He again wrote a memorial urging Yao Siren to petition for relief. Those he saved lived by the thousands and tens of thousands. Later, at forty, He became a presented scholar and rose to be minister of personnel.

Chen Gongcai once dreamed that a spirit said to him: You are a zui kui, and you will pass the examinations in successive degrees and rise to be grand coordinator. He awoke and told others. Someone said: Zui means the xinyou year. In the xinyou year he indeed passed the provincial examination, but failed the metropolitan examination. Astonished that the dream had not come true, he dreamed again, and the spirit said: The number of Heaven is fixed, but its turning rests with man. Thus when the Son of Heaven favors a great minister and gives him rank and emolument richly, if that minister does not do his loyal best, can the rank and emolument not be taken from him? Or if, trusting in favor, he is arbitrary and gives himself to killing, then it will reach even him. The number of Heaven and the law of the state are one. After your provincial degree you did five things by which you took bribes and damaged your virtue greatly. How can you complain that Heaven has taken away your blessing? From now on cultivate virtue, and perhaps you may keep your natural span. If not, your years will be taken as well. Chen wept, bowed, and awoke. He repented his faults and turned to good, and in the end closed his career as a prefectural instructor. Now the filial and incorrupt, the gongsheng and the tribute students, should cultivate their persons like jade and apply themselves to deeds that plant virtue; then to mount the degrees is but a step up to the next stair, and easy. How is it that they walk into the gate of power and profit, thinking only to have their hearts' pleasure and their will's fill, not knowing that a high literary talent may go unmet and fame and rank be blocked, and even that years may be cut short and life shortened? All of this is of that kind. Let those with aspiration turn back at once and cultivate themselves. As for the country gentry, they are the hope of the people. To do good while living at home can move the commandery and county, sway the villages, and foster the rising generation; their merit in transformation is a hundred times that of a scholar. Therefore to befriend the worthy and make goodness known, and to preside over the customs of the place, is the highest. To rectify one's person and lead by example, and to keep oneself quiet and content, is the next. Below that is to seek fields and ask after houses; below that is to cheat orphans and oppress widows; below that is to scheme for wealth and profit, and to speak on matters and pass money. That is the degeneration of the custom, and I dare not speak of it.

Wang Zao served as a penal clerk. Every day he brought gold home, and his wife suspected it was what he got by selling judgments. So she sent a maid with ten pieces of pig's trotter, and when he came home she lied to him, saying: She delivered thirteen pieces. Zao was angry that the maid had stolen, and questioned her severely, until she confessed under torture to what she had not done. Then his wife said: You bring money home every day, and I suspected you were forging cases by torture. So I made trial of you with the maid's affair. Under punishment, what will a man not confess? I beg that from today you bring home not one coin. Goods unjustly gained will surely bring guilt and blame after death. Zao was suddenly shaken into awakening, and sweat poured down his back. He wrote a poem, saying: The cangue and the rod come chasing only for gold; each turn but adds to the depth of resentful karma. From today I will not look back at the knife and the pen; I lay them down and return to wander in the bamboo grove. Thereupon he scattered all he had, abandoned his household, and studied the Way. Later he was confirmed as the Perfected One of Preserving Harmony.

Zhang Yisuo was a runner in the penal office of the capital. When he schemed out a warrant to arrest a man, he would move about with one enormous iron chain at his side. When he got money and was pleased, he would let the man go; if his desire was not quite satisfied, he would either privately hang and beat him, or falsely report to his own superior that this man's traces were secret and suspicious and that he should be sent to prison. Above he tied himself to the clerks, below he entangled the prison guards, and false accusation, terror, and extortion were his daily work. In three years he grew rich, and all men feared him and called him One Chain. At last he was seized by Censor Kong and put to death; his property was confiscated for the army, and his wife and daughters were sent to the women's quarters of the government. Among the clerks and runners in the yamens of today, there are many like Zhang Yisuo who gnash their teeth and suck blood. Those who have not yet entered should be urged to take up farming or trade; those who have entered should be urged to turn from evil and follow good. All who are kin or friends ought to give this their attention.

Zhang Hesi was a prison officer, greedy of bribes and cruel. Whenever he judged a prisoner, he would apply every punishment in turn; cangue, chain, manacle, and shackle, and the extremity of hardship and pain. When prisoners saw him, not one did not have his gall broken. He was called the Living Rakshasa. The sons and daughters born to him all had flesh cangues and flesh manacles, and died the moment they touched the ground. Later Hesi too was executed under the law. Again, there was a prison guard who was greedy and tyrannical toward the prisoners; they could not bear the suffering, and the guard would not stop until he had money. Afterward he had a son who also had a flesh cangue, and in a few years the child died, and the guard himself was beaten to death with the staff. Now of the sufferings of living men, those of prison are the greatest, and among them the misery of filth, crowding, and epidemic dysentery is worst in the summer months. In the capital there is each year the imperial order for the hot-season review, but there are none who carry it out. If a benevolent and worthy man could have it fixed as a standing rule that those whose sentences are not yet reduced be given a general clearing, and that for the heavily guilty held in custody a suitable secretarial officer be sent to sweep the prison, wash the cangues and manacles, and so extend the life-cherishing benevolence of the sagely sovereign; that in the summer months no indictments be received indiscriminately, no one be lightly kept in custody awaiting trial, the prison registers be consulted from time to time, the number of prisoners be checked, and clerks and runners be strictly forbidden to enter men's names for crimes without cause — then the pit of fire before one's eyes would be turned into a world of coolness. This depends only on those in authority: a movement of the thought, a movement of the tongue, a movement of the pen, and it is the work of a moment.

Alas! As all the foregoing sets forth, where is there not the evil of clerks and runners oppressing the people? You who shepherd the people — as you sleep soundly and dream sweetly within your yamen, do you ever think this far? Well did Zhu Shengzhi say: If the clerks are greedy, I do not hand my documents to their chambers; if the runners are greedy, I do not arrest and beat at random; if the jailers are greedy, I do not lightly put men in irons.

When two parties are in litigation before the law and right and wrong are not yet settled, life and death, giving and taking, hang upon a single word of mine. How can it be treated lightly? Yet now right and wrong are turned upside down, whether because of taking bribes, or because of yielding to private feeling, or else out of reckless and careless haste. If a man has any one of these, how can he be fit to hold office and stand above the people as their superior?

A certain Zhang served in Shu. He made cruelty the means of greed. In all the people's suits, he never asked what was right or wrong: if a man could bring a bribe, then the wrong side was also the right; if he could not, then the right side was also wrong. The people all ground their teeth at him. Later he lost office and went home, and was caught in a suit over a man's life; his son was unworthy, and his family property came to nothing, and he died of a foul disease.

Liu Anmin was a clerk of a county. He held his heart fair and even, and was respected by others. When the people had a suit, they would not go at once to the county office but would first go to him, to have right and wrong decided and the rights of the matter set out, and only then proceed. If he took the burden upon himself, he accepted it and did not decline. If it was right, he would say: This is right; it may be done. If it was wrong, he would enumerate it and say: This is wrong; to do it will surely bring loss. Thereby the litigation of the whole county was suddenly reduced. Afterward his two sons passed the examinations, and his family remains a great clan to this day.

Zhao Shi was an instructor in the prefecture of Wuwei. He dreamed of a prisoner who said: I was unfortunately done to death by Zu Xiang. Shi said: Zu Xiang knows the law well and is moreover upright and cautious. How could he have wronged you? The prisoner said: My death was indeed not Zu's intention, but because of one doubt of his the right and the wrong were never distinguished, and I was in the end sentenced to death. The resentment has its source; if not Xiang, then who? I have already complained in the dark court. Xiang has not long to live. In a little over a month he indeed died. In recent days false accusations and litigation are greatly in vogue. If one cannot transform the people by virtue, then if only the law of adding three degrees of penalty for false accusation were strictly enforced, litigation might perhaps be somewhat diminished. And even when there is litigation, it would not lead to a welter of doubtful and mistaken judgments. The worst evil lies with the plaintiffs at one's right and left, and with the careless coloring of the trial record, whereby the wind is fanned; they only fear it will too soon die down.

The Book says: Where guilt is doubtful, be lenient. It also says: Rather let a guilty man go free than that an innocent man be condemned. If then one deliberately turns a light offense into a heavy one, where is the sage's meaning of compassion in punishment? A human life is bound up with Heaven, and the officials concerned should attend to it most carefully. In this world there is the practice of false claims, which is exceedingly cruel. Men of the lower orders rely on it to play the rogue, until servants threaten their masters, stubborn tenants defy their landlords, and wives and concubines dominate their husbands. If some mishap occurs, then the village and clan seize the chance to roll up their sleeves, and the gentry thereupon whet their teeth: they plunder the household goods, insult the women, bind the corpse and pour in liquids, and crowd together to beat cruelly, all in order to seek bribes. Thus a son drives his mother to death, a wife in anger kills her husband; men rely on having many sons as the root of a claim to death, and mark out rich households as rich meat. Thus scholars and gentry become the kin of slaves and servants, and families of cap and gown become beggars. They plot in secret and give in the open, wrathful in the morning and pleased at evening. Thus there are those who maltreat the corpse and burn the bones, who trample in the door and wreck the house. The poor, resentful, and sullen stand by with hands in their sleeves, while the rich kinsmen suffer calamity and are condemned. The kinds of it are not easy to recount to the end. The officials of this world say only that one inspection at the place of death is enough to settle the grievance and give satisfaction, and who knows that the flesh is already pounded to a paste and rotten, and that whale-swallowing and tiger-devouring have reached this extreme? If this evil is not reformed, it will not only prompt men to kill themselves, but will make fathers and sons, brothers, take death for profit, expose corpses, and destroy the law. To weigh the circumstances is no different from killing a man with one's own hand. Truly such men deserve to be put to death by slow slicing. Now since it is hard to set the whole matter aside and ignore it, we should only strictly enforce the law of adding three degrees of penalty for false accusation. No matter how extreme the grievance or the pressure, whoever kills by poison but does not head the indictment with poisoning, or hangs himself or throws himself into water but does not head the indictment with hanging or drowning, shall be questioned according to the law, the aim being to punish one and warn a hundred. Let proclamations be posted to make this known. As for those who press a kinsman to death and make of it the foundation for a claim, when the truth of the matter is exposed, they should be punished all the more heavily. Those who seize the confusion to extort and cheat, or who falsely acknowledge a body and beat it, shall be strictly investigated and publicly proclaimed. Then the matter will be settled. And only when the matter is settled can right and wrong be discussed and the light and heavy weighed. Then the living will have no pain, the dead no blemish of disease, kin will have no heart for profit from death, and custom will have no evil of looting. What limit would there be to his secret virtue?

Nowadays, whenever men meet with a case of death, they never ask whether the circumstances are light or heavy, whether the matter is true or false. The bamboo plank is not enough, so they turn to the finger-press; that is not enough, so they turn to the leg-press; and there are even those who beat a hundred strokes and more. Under such pain, what confession cannot be had? And even if the man is later sentenced to execution, at this moment he will beg only for a little delay. Are there no benevolent men in the world who can feel a pang at this? Zhu Risheng said: False claims founded on a death are even more prevalent in the customs of the south. When I was magistrate of Wucheng, I punished this evil severely. I issued a separate form for cases of death, in which the day and hour and the circumstances were to be written plainly, and it was not permitted to use at once the quibbling phrases and the cunning words. On the back of the form were printed the front, the back, the left side, and the right side, together with the single sheet for the wounds on the corpse, and the complainant was made to fill them in himself. It was passed in with the drum and accepted at any hour. I myself went at once to the place of death, questioned according to the written words, and inspected according to the chart. I did not hand the matter over to assistants or entrust it to clerks and coroners. If it was indeed a true wound, sentence was passed according to law; if it was a false claim, the man was severely punished at once. As for hanging oneself, throwing oneself into water, falling by mischance, and the like, these again were dealt with according to the circumstances, and the order was given for immediate burial, so as to cut off the misery of extortion and entanglement. Even in the height of summer's heat or the depth of winter's cold, in mountain nooks and watery hollows, I did not once shrink or delay. Therefore within two years no one came to complain of a death. Ah! The matter of a human life concerns life and death; how can one be other than careful?

Li Ruoshui was judicial officer of Huainan. At that time there were five robbers who, their affair having failed, were imprisoned, and they said that they had once been in league with a monk named Zicheng. Afterward the five were executed, and the monk had just been released. The monk said that he had in truth never been a robber. Ruoshui could have dealt with him leniently; instead he held firmly that the robbers' words were true and killed him cruelly. In a little over a month the jailer Li Neng cried out without cause: Monk, this is no affair of mine; it was only the judicial officer who drove me to it. Having said this, he died. The next day the assistant judge Liu Yuan also died. The day after that Ruoshui died suddenly, and the whole household was all but extinguished.
The assistant judge Liu Yuan also died, and one day after that Li Ruoshui died suddenly, and his whole family was all but wiped out.

Lord Zhao Qingxian of the Song was military adviser of the Wu'an commandery. There was a man who had forged a seal, and the clerks all said he should die. The lord alone said: The forging was done before the amnesty; the use was after it. There was no use before the amnesty, and no forging after it. By the law he does not die. And so, because of the doubt, he released him. Later, when he governed Chengdu, there was a Li Xiaozhong who gathered two hundred men and privately made ordination certificates to ordain men as monks. Someone reported it as treason, and the case was complete. The lord did not give it to the law officers but decided it himself, sentencing Xiaozhong for privately making the certificates and sparing the rest from death. The matter was noised abroad in the capital, and it was said the lord had let a treasonable faction go. The court took the trial record and examined it, and in the end found nothing to alter. Later he retired as junior guardian of the heir apparent, and his son Wan was also eminent. Mao Qizong said: To press what belongs before the amnesty as though it were after it is likewise of the kind that turns a light matter into a heavy one. Well said Yin Wenzhuang: The edict pardons the guilty, and yet the judgments proceed as before; the edict remits arrears, and yet the pressing for taxes grows the more urgent. The gracious intent is dammed up, and the people of Heaven have no way to receive its moisture. This is what benevolent and worthy men grind their teeth over and sicken at heart.

Guo Hong of the Later Han studied the law, and the governor Kou Xun made him an officer of judgments. For thirty years he judged cases and applied the law fairly and with forbearance, so that the people had no resentful feelings. He was likened to Lord Yu of Donghai. He died at ninety-five. His son Gong transmitted his father's calling from youth. Later he was appointed commandant of justice. The Gong family for generations held the law in their hands and made it their business to be lenient and even. When he came to preside over the judicial officers and to judge cases, he was greatly given to pity and forbearance. So he set out in order the several heavy articles that could be dealt with leniently, forty-one items in all, and memorialized them; all were put into effect and written into the statutes. Gong, in presenting and judging cases, saved and kept alive a great many. For several generations afterward the family all transmitted the law, and their eminence and prosperity were without equal.

The Admonition on Lessening Punishment. Do not give rein to authority and indulge your own will, making the state's statutes fit my anger and my pleasure. Do not bend to private feeling and overturn the law, looking on the people's lives as on a writhing worm. Do not, because a man glares and holds his neck stiff and stammers and stumbles in speech, straightway add to him the crime of juggling the statutes with cunning slander. At the head of the staff, man and ghost are judged; beneath the pen, death and life are joined. Pull out one hair and he knows the pain; bite one finger and he knows the pity. For one day's labor under the rod, three seasons' ploughing hangs in the balance. When one man is bound in the prison gate, eight mouths go without food and clothing. The moving and the growing are all lives; flesh and blood all concern Heaven. Therefore it was that in Donghai the fame of benevolence endured for a million years.

The Admonition on Lessening Fines. Do not take the money with which the people sell their children and pawn their wives to fatten your wife and children. Do not seize the wealth with which the people ruin their families and break up their property to enrich your house and lands. Do not gather up the people's resentful cries of hunger and cold and their appeals beating against the ground to furnish your banquets of song and laughter. One redemption is a hundred mu of tax; one sheet of paper is ten days of gruel. One grain is the blood of the ploughman, through how much frost and bitter sourness. One thread of silk is the weaver woman's tears, through how many nights and days of eating and sleeping. In the offices the days of piled fat; for the poor and black-haired, years of aching heads. The gods cannot be deceived; the way of Heaven quickly returns. Therefore it was that Yang Baiqi's pure wind became a fish-trap for ten thousand ages.

Zengzi said: If you get at the truth of the matter, then grieve and be pitiful, and do not rejoice. These words mean that for a guilty man, at the time he receives punishment, one should still trace the true circumstances of his offense; one must not add punishment at will. How much less, since the dead cannot come back to life! Though his guilt was of his own taking, yet at the sight of it the heart is wounded, and one has not even time to cover the face and wipe away the tears — what is the use of adding anger? It is the extreme of a hardened heart. As for the six kinds of domestic animals, the birds, and the fish, when they are killed by men, one should all the more pity them as guiltless and innocent and find means to save and protect them. To see them and add anger is to be no more than a cruel and slaughter-loving wicked man.

Lu Duoxun of the Song was banished to Zhuyai. Li Fu, a grand master of remonstrance, went in to see Zhao Pu, and said that although Zhuyai lies beyond the sea, its water and soil have no other evil, and those exiled there mostly survive, whereas Chunzhou lies within the interior, yet those who go there surely die; he begged that the former order be recalled and changed, so that outwardly it might display leniency while in truth the man was put in a place of death. Pu nodded. In a little over a month Li Fu was charged with some matter, banished to Chunzhou, and died when he reached the commandery.

Yang Daosheng was an army adviser to the Prince of Shaoling. He had an elder brother, Haizhen, who was governor of Chazhou. He asked for leave to visit him, and at the parting the brother gave him a farewell feast. He saw a man bound to a tree, who wept and begged Daosheng, saying: Chazhou means to kill me; I beg you to seek my release. Daosheng asked what his crime was, and he said: I planned to desert and rebel. Daosheng said in anger: This is the most hateful of all. He straightway cut out the man's eyes with the dagger at his belt and swallowed them. In a moment his brother arrived and gave the order for him to be beheaded. Then Daosheng felt the eyes stuck in his throat and would not go down, until gradually it swelled and choked him; on the road he could not eat, and died.

In the Spring and Autumn period, Gao Zigao of Wei had a prisoner's foot cut off. At the time of the amputation his face was sorrowful. Later, in the troubles of Kuai Kui, Zigao fled. The man whose foot had been cut was keeping the gate, and said to him: There is a gap over there. Zigao said: A gentleman does not climb over. The man said: There is a hole over there. He said: A gentleman does not crawl through. Again the man said: There is a room over there. And so he entered it. When the pursuers gave up, Zigao said: I with my own hands cut off your foot, and you have let me escape three times. Why? The man whose foot was cut said: To have my foot cut off was indeed my crime; but your honor's face was sorrowful at the amputation — was it that you bore me a private liking? It is Heaven that gives birth to a gentleman, and his way is thus by nature. This is why I have saved your honor today.

Zhang Qing was a prison clerk. He was compassionate and careful, and held himself in check. When the instruments of punishment were used, he would bathe; in the summer months he swept and sprinkled all the more diligently. He used to warn men, saying: When a man breaks the law, how could it be what he would choose? Food and drink and bedding must be made finer and cleaner. He had always honored the Buddha, and whenever a prisoner was executed he would keep the vegetarian fast for him and devoutly recite the scriptures and invoke the Buddha, praying that he might escape suffering and be reborn. His other hidden merits were very many. He lived to eighty-three and died without illness. His sons and grandsons afterward became eminent officials.

Liu Xiyuan of the Ming once dreamed that a man bowed to him and said: I am Cao Han, a general of the Song. Long ago, in the Tang, I was a petty clerk, and because I heard a Dharma master preach the scriptures and was moved, I gave one vegetarian feast. From that time I received the recompense of never losing the cap and gown in life after life, and gradually accumulated good causes, until in the Song I became a deputy general. Because of the slaughter of a city and the killing of men without cause, I was born life after life as a pig to repay those I had killed. In a former year my tenant farmer gave me to your honor in payment of rent, and by your honor's pity I was kept alive. Now I am again here repaying the debt, and I have come especially to beg for rescue. The lord said: By what means can you be saved? He said: Whenever the time of slaughter and cutting comes, the suffering is past bearing; only when I hear the sound of the Buddha's name is the suffering loosed. I beg your honor, whenever you see the hour of killing, or the time of cooking and boiling, to rouse the great compassionate heart and simply invoke Amitabha Buddha, or hold the Great Compassion Mantra or the Cundi Mantra. It will not only loose my suffering but also bring the benefit of deliverance. Having said this, he sorrowed, gave thanks, and went away. Again, Zheng Lin died suddenly, and because he had been summoned by mistake was sent back. The King of Hell said: Return to the world of the living and strive to do good. When you see men killing living creatures, only invoke Namo Amitabha Buddha and Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva. They will receive birth, and you will also gain blessing. From this we know that invoking the Buddha can deliver the dead; in this life it can increase blessing and long life, and after death one will surely be born in the West. Someone may ask: If one merely invokes the Buddha's name, how does it benefit both oneself and others? I answer: Living beings are deluded as to their own nature and have no term for awakening; but once they hear the Buddha's name, it is as though one in the dark were roused. Moreover, when they kill living creatures with cruelty, and I invoke the Buddha with compassion, then the road of forsaking evil and following good lies precisely here. Therefore to invoke the Buddha at the sight of killing is merit without measure. The great master Hanshan of the Ming said: In my ordinary life, whenever I hear the sound of slaughter, I cannot help a pain at the heart, and at once I invoke the Buddha and the Rebirth Mantra. I used to think I was but doing my own heart's utmost. Now, seeing this case, I know that the one who suffers truly gains benefit and joy. Extending this further: whenever one sees killing or hears killing, or sees the things of the butcher's block and the cauldron and the knife, at whatever time and in whatever place, one should rouse this heart — compassion at every turn of the eye, deliverance from suffering at every thought. If all the people of the world could rouse this samadhi of the compassionate heart, it would all be the work of bodhisattvas saving living beings. How could its merit be conceived?

Punishment and prison are the great affairs of a state; the life and death of the people hang upon them. Therefore when the Most High set forth his words, he strictly forbade the taking of bribes, and in the matter of the crooked and the straight, the light and the heavy, he gave his intent especially to those who question and sentence, because those in power can more easily do what is convenient. Yet the eyes and ears of one man are limited, and clerks, secretaries, and runners who can put away their evil habits and, leaning on the authority of the officials, do good, saving men from trouble and calamity, will create merit and virtue without measure or bound. Now good and evil part ways in the subtlety of a single thought, and to use the wind to fill one's sail is to borrow a force that makes it easier. Men say the public gate may not be entered; I say the public gate is a good place to practice. Could the words of the ancients have been deceiving me? As for killing men and killing creatures — men killing, I killing — it is all one killing. Even if one cannot meet a creature and save it alive, can it be that to invoke the Buddha with a devout heart costs wealth and effort and so cannot be done? Think of it, think of it.

Manjushri Bodhisattva said to the Buddha: If a man does evil in his youth and cultivates in old age, can he still attain buddhahood? The Buddha said: The sea of suffering has no bound; turn the head and the shore is there. Chan Master Yuanwu said: Who is without fault? To have faulted and be able to mend it — no good is greater. Only the gentleman can mend his faults and turn to good, and so his virtue is renewed day by day. The petty man hides his evil and glosses over his wrongs, and so his wickedness is the more manifest. The petty man's faults are sure to be glossed over; therefore the Most High earnestly warned against it. He Longtu said: There are faults of the mouth, faults of the body, faults of the mind. He who would well mend his evil should only be alert and awake, strive to put away his clinging and stinginess, examine and probe into the finest point, strip away and change to the very bottom, and refine his cultivation without cease, until in the crooked he attains sincerity. The learning of the sages, the learning of the Buddha, the learning of the mystery — all are deep and subtle and not easy to speak of. Yet the method of learning from below, which runs through all three teachings, is nothing but mending one's faults.

Sima Wengong of the Song, when he was five years old, could not get the skin off a walnut. A maid took it off with hot water. His elder sister came in from outside and asked about it, and the boy said: I took it off myself. His father scolded him, saying: How can a little boy tell lies? The boy was startled and repented, and in all his life he never dared to lie.

Xu Jiexiao Ji of the Song, when he first saw Master Anding, held his head a little askew. Anding said in a stern voice: The head must be held straight. The boy at once repented and awoke, saying: The head must be held straight — how much more must the heart be straight! From that time he never once bent his heart. When men asked him the essentials of establishing oneself and conducting oneself, he would always write in large characters the two words upright and straight and give it to them.

Zeng Zigong of the Song was on good terms with Wang Jinggong. Emperor Shenzong asked Zigong about Wang Anshi. He said: Anshi's writings and conduct are not inferior to Yang Xiong's; it is because he is stingy that he does not come up to him.
