The emperor said: Anshi makes light of wealth and honor — why do you call him stingy? Zigong said: What your servant calls stinginess is that Anshi is brave in doing and stingy in mending his faults. Emperor Shenzong nodded. Anshi had the talent of a king's assistant, and yet in the end, by persisting in his errors, brought calamity flowing down upon the ancestral shrines and the cursing of ten thousand generations. How much more for the obstinate and untalented men of today, who day after day are in the midst of their faults and do not know to mend them!

Take the small so as to accomplish the great; accumulate one so as to complete a hundred million. Therefore goodness is prized for being accumulated. To know it is to do it; to do it one should put forth strength. Laozi said: A nine-storied terrace begins with a heap of earth; a journey of a thousand li begins beneath the foot. If a man mends one fault a day, he dissolves one karma of sin; if he does one good deed a day, he adds one foundation of blessing. The Perfected Lady of Purple Emptiness said: The Way is born of quiet stillness; virtue is born of humility and yielding; blessing is born of purity and frugality; life is born of harmony and ease; trouble is born of many desires; fault is born of lightness and contempt. Guard the eye: do not look at others' wrongs. Guard the mouth: do not speak of others' shortcomings. Guard the mind: do not give rein to greed and anger. Guard the body: do not follow evil companions. Life and destiny are like a candle in the wind; ever think of the body after this body. This form lodges for a while in the dust of the world; do not create karma within karma. Therefore good and evil both abide in the spiritual storehouse, clear and undimmed to the least fraction. A man may be cunning in his schemes, but Heaven is more cunning in its retribution. Seen from this, if a man in the course of a single day hears one good word, sees one good deed, or does one good act, that day has not been passed in vain. As for him who knows the good and does it not, I know not what lungs and guts he has; he willingly casts himself away, trifles away the days and wastes the months, and cuts himself off from Heaven. He too is a fool.

Chan Master Tianru Ze of the Yuan, in a general discourse, said: The old teaching says: I see others die, and my heart burns like fire; it is not that I burn for others — soon it will be my turn. Words like these — who does not know them? Knowing, one does indeed know; it is only that one will not cultivate. If I say you will not cultivate, that would be to wrong you. Most of the great virtuous ones before me have set to work and done the practice; it is only that they have not reached the ground of a hundredfold completion. Where does the fault lie? The fault lies in not being brave, not being diligent, not being firm, not enduring long. For a while one rouses the will, and before long one retreats again. Therefore it is said: The Buddha-dharma is not much; it is only that men who last long are hard to find. Study the Way as at the first, and there is more than enough to become a buddha. To be unchanging from beginning to end — that is a true great man. How many such are there today? Often of ten men, five pairs are all of the sort whose hearts retreat from the Way. If one examines the causes and conditions of their retreating hearts, each of them too has something that weighs him down. What are the weights? There are three kinds of weight. The first, whether monk or lay, man or woman, every one is weighed down by the mouth that must be fed. Next, those who have family dependents are weighed down by their dependents. Those who have household affairs are weighed down by their household affairs. These three weights weigh all the men of the world to death. All the men of the world, meeting these three weights, have busied themselves for a lifetime, clamored for a lifetime, suffered for a lifetime, schemed and muddled for a lifetime, and passed a lifetime in vain. How much more that because of these three weights they have roused greed, anger, and delusion without measure and created evil karma great and small without measure. By the retribution of that karma they fall into the sea of suffering of the three evil paths and the eight difficulties, and in birth and death and the wheel of rebirth endure suffering and affliction without measure and gain no deliverance. And though they endure suffering without measure, they are unchanging from first to last in this: they do not awake. That they do not awake is because they do not understand. What do they not understand? They do not understand that this body, these dependents, and these household affairs are none of them yours. If I now tell you that the body is not yours, you will not yet believe it. This mountain monk will set it out fully for you from the beginning and break it open. When you first came into your mother's womb, at the moment of conception, there was only a single consciousness-spirit; how was there ever a body? This body is but a lump of stubborn flesh formed from the union of your father's white and your mother's red. It is in itself without knowing or feeling; it does not know pain, does not know itch, does not know cold, does not know heat, does not know hunger, does not know fullness, does not know suffering, does not know joy. Because of your one consciousness-spirit, it settles in this lump of stubborn flesh; and from then on it knows itch and pain, knows cold and heat, knows hunger and fullness, knows suffering and joy. And when it has come forth from the womb, you simply take it for yourself and call it my body. If one tells you that the body is not yours, you will certainly not believe it. Therefore the buddhas and patriarchs pitied you and again with bitter words said to you: This is not your body. This is a stinking skin bag formed of essence and blood. It is not under your management, not at your disposal; and even birth, old age, sickness, and death are not yours to arrange.

How do we know it is so? Take the time when you were first conceived and dwelt in your mother's womb: every seven days came a change, and by degrees you grew — the five viscera and six bowels, the hundred bones and nine orifices, the four limbs and six senses, sinew, bone, skin, and flesh, gradually taking form, and at last coming forth from the womb. All of it was blown by the hot wind and driven by the power of karma; you were unaware and unknowing — how was any of it at your disposal? After you were born and had been nourished to thirty or forty years, then the hair turns white, the teeth loosen, the face yellows, the flesh thins; by degrees it changes, by degrees it ages. The signs of age appear, and sickness follows; when sickness has come, death comes. All such changes and decays are not one of them yours. You yourself do not wish it so, but there is no help for it: you cannot manage it. Consider: from birth to death, upon this stinking skin bag, how much affection and love you have spent, tending it in every way, cherishing it in every way, doctoring and arranging it in every way. And it repays you with ingratitude, and is so hateful. And there is something yet more hateful. Take the burning heat of midsummer: there is a strong and healthy fellow who suddenly, at dusk, takes a fatal illness and dies. By the second watch of the night the stench is already choking, and no one can come near. They hurry to put him in a coffin and shut the lid, and before the bell sounds and the sky is light they hurry to carry him out and burn him. Even the closest and dearest dependents cannot be kept to stay. Seen from this: last night he was still a healthy fellow, and this morning he is a pinch of bone ash. Who knows where that one consciousness-spirit has gone? Such a swift change is not yours at all. If it were your body, it ought to be yours to manage. Since it is not yours to manage, how can you falsely take it for your body and suffer yourself to be weighed down by it and let your mind for the Way retreat? Your dependents are the same. Each drags a stinking skin bag; neither is free, neither can manage the other. When impermanence comes, neither can take the other's place. All your life long, before your eyes, the two of you are bound about by a kind of affection and call each other dependents. But once the eyes are closed, neither knows the other any more. How then can you falsely take him for your dependent and suffer yourself to be weighed down by him and let your mind for the Way retreat? Your household affairs are the same. While your eyes are open and your legs are strong, you calculate and manage, hoard and guard, thinking that for a hundred thousand years you will have the use of them. Who knows that when the single breath does not come back, not one hair of it can be taken along? How then can you falsely take them for your household affairs, and suffer yourself to be weighed down and let your mind for the Way retreat? Now that you have heard these words, you should turn the light around and see through them, and bitterly awake yourselves. On these three kinds of weight, do not recognize them, do not cling to them, do not crave them. Settle in your allotted portion, let things run their course and pass the time. But you must turn the thought around, and on the matter of birth and death rouse up bravery and diligence, be firm and enduring, and seek to see clearly. Then the abbot, ashamed of his own poor talent, may still have chattered on and on and uttered all these shallow and commonplace words, and made himself a laughingstock to the adept. And yet, if he is an adept, he will not laugh. A rustic song of the village fields — sorrow and joy are each heard by each.

Su Cheng of the Tang was by nature stubborn and vicious, and in all his life there was not one good thing to be said of him. When he saw fine words and noble conduct in books, he would point to them as embellished talk; when he saw men diligently practicing good deeds, he would laugh at them as villainy. When he was grown, his body gradually shrank, and he walked on the ground on both hands, and slept and ate with the dogs. After a year he died.

Duke Huan of Qi of the Zhou passed by the ruins of the Guo family and asked an old man: How did the Guo family perish? He answered: By loving the good and hating the evil. The duke said: Loving the good and hating the evil — how did that destroy them? He said: They loved the good but could not act, and hated the evil but could not put it away. Seen from this: men today are deluded as to their own spirit-consciousness and do not understand their own nature. The ten thousand conditions assail them and they must respond on eight sides. One thought comes, one thought goes; in a single day and night there are eight hundred and forty million thoughts, like wind in the air with no place to rest, like a stone pressing on grass that stops and springs up again. How can they have a day of single-minded goodness? Therefore even when they know that good ought to be done, they are shifted by the desires of things; and though they discourse on the scriptures and preach the Dharma all day long, they most often carry the leaf away while losing the root, and sit still to be tripped and fall. Is this not deeply to be lamented?

When a crime is one's own, and the affair comes to light, one then drags others in — what the proverb calls pulling a man into the water. The intent is either to gloss over a leak or to settle a score. Who knows that one's own fault can in the end never be concealed, and that another man can in the end never be falsely accused — one but creates sin within sin? Though one escape the king's law, it is hard to escape the punishment of Heaven.

Zhao Ye once watched Jia Yi kill an ox. When Yi died, he dragged Ye in to share the guilt. Ye was brought to the dark court and could scarcely make himself clear. Suddenly a mirror appeared, a full fathom across, hanging in the air, in which could be seen plainly Jia Yi wielding the knife, while Ye, standing behind the door, had on his face a look of unwillingness to bear it. Then Yi submitted, and Ye was able to return. According to the Buddha's word, in all the world birth and death follow one upon another, and at the time of death, before the warmth has left the body, the good and evil of a whole life all appear at once. For the most part the state that appears at the end is the state of one's own mind in ordinary days. The King of Hell's mirror of karma is my own mind's mirror. And if today one does a single unkind thing, has it not been coming and going in the breast? How then can one falsely drag in another?

The arts and techniques — such as medicine, divination, astrology, and physiognomy, and every single craft and skill — are all of this kind. The shallow use them to nourish life; the high use them to succor the world. If one dams them up and prevents them from being practiced, that too is the narrowness of our Way, and there will be many in the four quarters who are hungry and cold and without work. As for depraved teachers and quack physicians who injure the teaching and ruin lives, and alchemists of the cinnabar furnaces and the like, these may not be cited under this head; they are what ought to be prohibited. And households of scholars and commoners must keep their doors pure and strict: the three kinds of nuns and the six kinds of old women should all be cut off, and even if there be comings and goings, one should look at the person. This is truly the way to make the root sincere and to stop things at the subtle point.

In his lifetime Zhai Ganyou was famous for summoning spirits. He often thought that in the whole county of Yun'an there were fifteen perilous places on the river, and so he summoned the shoal spirits to level them. Fourteen answered the summons, but one shoal was in the charge of a goddess in a high cap and wide sleeves, who spoke out with feeling: By your honor's intent, you mean only to make things convenient for boats and oars. But you do not know that those who work boats and oars make double profit every day, and even if there be some small cost, it is not enough to injure them. Along the river there are three or four hundred households of humble folk who have no fields to plough and no mulberry to feed silkworms; they depend wholly on hauling and carrying to keep alive. If now all the shoals and rapids are leveled, it will indeed be very convenient for boats and oars — but what of the food and clothing of these humble folk? The intent of the Most High must not be so. I deeply fear that in time to come guilt will be incurred, and that you will not escape entanglement. You would do well to weigh it further. The Celestial Master sighed and said: What you have considered is beyond my reach. Thereupon he commanded the fourteen shoal spirits each to restore their rapids. Seen from this, it is not only the arts and techniques that must not be dammed up. For all such as live by the strength of their bodies, one should especially find means to keep the way open; do not exhaust their strength, do not press their skill to the end. Leave a margin of ground everywhere, so that they do not come to straits in hunger and cold. Such is the heart of a benevolent man.

To slander is to mock and insult; to defame is to blame and disparage. There are two kinds of slanderers and defamers. One is the foolish and deluded, who are blind to its shadow and echo; this is called hating Heaven from inside a jar. The other is the clever and eloquent, who fan the wind and the waves; this is called catching the moon in the water. The sages and worthies are the three teachings of Confucianism, Buddhism, and Daoism. The Confucians set up their teaching by rectitude; the Buddhists set up theirs by greatness; the Daoists set up theirs by reverence. If we look at their love of life and hatred of killing, it is one benevolence. To look on others as oneself is one impartiality. To check anger and curb desire, to forbid faults and guard against wrong, is one discipline. To be thunder to the deaf multitudes and sun and moon to the blind, is one transforming influence. To speak in terms of the coarse traces, the principles of the world are no more than the two roads of good and evil, and the meaning of the three teachings is nothing but to teach men to change from evil to good. To speak in terms of the method of the mind-ground, then all return to one. Therefore Emperor Xiaozong of the Song, in his Discourse on the Origin of the Way, said: Use Buddhism to govern the mind, Daoism to govern the body, Confucianism to govern the world. If one truly knows that mind, body, and world cannot be left with any one of them ungoverned, how can the three teachings be allowed to have any one of them not established? The Confucians of today either use the sages to refute the Buddha, or set the Buddha above the sages. The monks and Daoists of today either destroy Daoism for the sake of Buddhism, or dispute against Buddhism for the sake of Daoism. All of it is the view of self and the duality of subject and object, wrongly dividing the great Way. Do they not know that the three teachings are in origin neither the same nor different, and that the only trouble is the vain arising of private opinion, the measuring of things by private intent, the racing of a floating heart in argument? One of the highest wisdom, if he can truly level his heart and blend them, and probe straight to the source, will know that the Buddha's clarifying of the mind and seeing of the nature, his going from delusion and seeking of awakening, the Daoist's clearing of the heart and diminishing of desire, his piling up of merit and practice of conduct, and the Confucian's extending of knowledge and investigating of things, his rectifying of the heart and making sincere of the will — all embrace and transform in many directions, and there is nothing discordant in them. In the end they come down to leading men into the Way, and no more. What name or form is there to be clung to? Therefore we know that the true Dharma of the three teachings is together the eye of all living beings for ten thousand generations. Why should those who slander it make for themselves the cause of having their tongues torn out? As for the classics and scriptures, the books, and written paper — they are where the spirit of the sages and worthies lodges. Those who trample on them are guilty of the same crime as the slanderer.

I have observed that China's possession of the three teachings is like the naming of Heaven, Earth, and Man as the three powers, and of ruler and minister, father and son, husband and wife as the three bonds: for a single moment they cannot do without one another. From the time Fuxi drew the trigrams, Confucianism was already beginning. Now Confucianism in China can make the constant relations upright and human relations clear, can make rites and music, punishments and government reach in all four directions without disorder, and at the last can bring it about that Heaven and Earth and the myriad things each attain its place. Its merit to this world is great. Therefore the First Emperor of Qin wished to do away with the Confucians, and the Confucians could not be done away with. If they could not be done away with, could they be slandered? Some men see only Gongsun Hong's crooked learning that fawned on the times, Zhu Qinming's sweeping away of the Five Classics, Yang Ziyun's awakening to the wonder of the Great Mystery and his flattery of the usurper Wang Mang, Xu Jingzong's knowledge of the meaning of the Diqiu and his loss of integrity to the false Wu — all of these came forth from the Confucians, and yet they were in truth the criminals of Confucianism. How can one, because such men flowed into worthlessness, thereupon slander the sages and worthies who established the teaching? Again, from the time Laozi passed through the pass, Daoism had already begun. Now Daoism in China can make a man keep to purity and emptiness, be tranquil and retiring in his own pasture, wash away the habits of a welter of entanglements, and at the last reach quiet silence and non-doing and return to his heavenly truth. Its merit to the teaching of the world is supreme. Therefore Emperor Wu of Liang strove to abolish Daoism, and Daoism could not be abolished. If it could not be abolished, could it be slandered? Some men see only the rat Daoist deceiving Su Dongpo with a midnight trick; Lin Lingsu deluding Emperor Huizong with a dream of the divine Empyrean; Zheng Huaji, immortal of heaven, doing no more than making great boasts to deceive the world; He Deyi, immortal of earth, in the end adorning fraud to steal a name — all of these came forth from the Daoists, and yet they were in truth the criminals of Daoism. How can one, because such men flowed into depraved arts, thereupon slander the sages and worthies who raised up the teaching? And so at last, when Emperor Ming of the Han was moved by a dream of a golden man, Buddhism arose. Now Buddhism in China can make a man cast off the ornate and approach the real, put away the false and keep the true, and go from forceful practice to effortless practice, beginning with benefiting himself and ending with benefiting others, until at the last he beholds all with compassion and makes equal the resentful and the dear. What the living people rely upon in it is supreme. Therefore Emperor Wu of Wei exceedingly wished to destroy Buddhism, and Buddhism could not be destroyed. If it could not be destroyed, could it be slandered? Some men see only that the mantras of the Hu monks could not prevail against Fu Yi — Fu Yi slandered the Buddha and recklessly cited rumors, and men of later times, not seeing through it, took them for authentic records; this is truly to be pitied — that the radiance shown by the stone Buddha could not move the Cheng brothers; that the Buddha's tooth, for all its spiritual power, was broken by the horn of an antelope; that the Buddha's tooth, for all its divinity, was destroyed by Zhao Feng's axe; and that the White Lotus and the Wuwei sects ran riot, and the empty falsehood of the Xiang and Luo families — one raised the cry and the crowd answered. All of these came forth from the Buddhists, and yet they were in truth the criminals of Buddhism. How can one, because such men flowed into outer demons, thereupon slander the sages and worthies who transmitted the teaching?

Li Zhuowu of the Ming loved to defame the sages and worthies. He once made up two sayings. The first was: If Heaven had not given birth to Confucius, the whole of antiquity would have been as a long night. The other was: Then from Fuxi and the ancient emperors downward, did all men walk by burning torches? Next he came to Mencius and on to the Cheng brothers and Zhu Xi, and his slander was all the more extreme. Afterward he was charged with a crime and died in prison.

The Lord Emperor Wenchang said: The scholars who are enrolled in my register all come from reverencing written words. The father of Wang Yigong of the Song, when he saw written paper cast away, would always pick it up, wash it with clean water, and burn it. One evening he dreamed that the Sage of Declaration stroked his back and said: You reverence my teaching. It is a pity you are already old; I shall send Zeng Shen to be born in your house. In his late years he had a son, whom he named Zeng, and who became a famous chief minister. Again, Yang Baihang of Luzhou used the sacred writings as a seat, and his whole family was afflicted with leprosy; Xianyu Kun of Changjun mutilated Mencius, and his whole household perished; Yang Quanshan buried written paper, and for five generations his family passed the examinations; Li Zicai buried written paper, and in his own person became an eminent official. The retribution is clear before men's eyes and ears. How can one fail to reverence and cherish it? The poem says: Written paper in the world is the same as the stored scriptures; whoever sees it must commit it to the fire, or send it to the long stream or bury it in pure earth. So shall blessing and long life be given you without end. It also says: Reverence and cherish written paper and give it to water and fire; everyone knows the karma of good. Who has no household with shoe patterns and ledgers? It is well only when they are exchanged for white paper.

Gao Zhishou did not believe in the immortals and the buddhas, and reviled and defamed them to the utmost. He once pasted over a wall with the Lotus Sutra, and when men gave him a jade Buddha he said: This can serve as a vessel, and had it sawn up into ten rings. Afterward, because he slandered the government of the court, an edict was issued sending him to the ministry of justice for interrogation, and he was cut in two at the waist in the marketplace.

Qi Jiguang of the Ming always held to the Diamond Sutra. He suddenly dreamed of a dead soldier who begged him to recite one scroll to aid his lot in the dark world. The duke rose in the morning and recited it through, and dreamed again that the soldier said: I have received your honor's great grace, but I obtained only half a scroll, because in the midst of it two words were mixed in that were of no use. The duke thought over the reason, and it was that when a maid brought tea and cakes, he had waved his hand to refuse them; though he did not speak, in his heart there were the two words not wanted. The next morning he shut the door and recited the scripture, and dreamed again that the soldier thanked him, saying: I have obtained deliverance. Now if even a single mixed thought will not do, how much less mockery and insult?

Zhao Juyi kept the Jade Emperor Scripture but had not given up wine and meat. He died suddenly, and the King of the Dark Court asked him: What good did you do in your life? He answered: From youth I have kept the Jade Emperor Scripture. The king rose, joined his palms, and said: Such merit is the very highest. Your term shall be extended. He also said: The heaviest guilt is the killing of living creatures. Why did you fill your kitchen with pigs and sheep? Thereupon he commanded a guard to drive a long nail into Juyi's head. Juyi silently invoked the precious title of the Jade Emperor, and golden light covered his body, and the nail went in no further. When he revived, he gave up his household and entered the Way, and afterward became an immortal. Again it is told that the Prince of Jingling, when gravely ill, because he revered and trusted the Surangama Sutra, had a golden arm pour broth for him; and Lu Jingyu, held in prison, because he single-mindedly recited the Heart Sutra, had his cangue and manacles fall off of themselves. When the Diamond Sutra was carried with one morning and evening, the miner escaped the calamity of the underground pit; when the Lotus Sutra was held in the mind without cease, the concubine Su escaped the peril of the river waves. For those who revere and trust the sages and worthies, there has never been one who did not obtain the recompense of the sages and worthies.

The men of moral conduct in the world — such as the scholars who read the books and understand principle, and the monks and Daoists who cultivate with bitter effort — their words are a pattern and their deeds a model; they transcend their rank and stand out from their kind, and are wherein the upright spirit of Heaven and Earth gathers. There is no time even to love and reverence them; how can one invade and insult them?

When Chan Master Guoqing was preaching the Dharma, there was one who was a provincial intendant of the circuit and had never believed in the Buddha. He had the master bound and given twenty strokes of the staff. That night he dreamed of his dead father, who wept and said in anger: How dare you insult the Chan master? The King of the Dark Court has given me twenty strokes of the iron whip and has struck away your office.

Chunyu Chongde at twenty entered the prefectural school. His nature was depraved and perverse. Whenever there was a man of moral conduct among the scholars, he would certainly insult and revile him without restraint. One night he suddenly saw a spirit, who said: You have schemed a hundred ways to invade and insult men of moral conduct; therefore I have come to take away your wisdom. Having said this, he took a knife and struck once. Chongde fell unconscious, and when he revived he was in the end like a fool. A few years later he died.

When Zhang Liang of the Han was young, he was walking at Xiapi. On the bridge was an old man whose shoe had fallen down below the bridge, and he said to Liang: Boy, go down and fetch my shoe. Liang thought of his age and forced himself to go down and fetch it. The old man again lifted his foot and said: Boy, put the shoe on me. Liang thereupon knelt and put it on. The old man said: A boy who can be taught. He brought out a scroll of writing and said: Read this, and you can be the teacher of kings. Then he went away and did not return. When Liang looked at the book, it was the Military Art of the Grand Duke. From this he studied and read it, and assisted Emperor Gaozu to take the world, and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Liu. Seen from this, men of moral conduct complete other men's talents in many ways. Those who invade and insult them are like one who raises dust against the wind or blocks the sky with a bare hand: one mostly sees that he does not know his own measure.

Shooting is not only the use of bow and arrow. Firelocks, bird guns, poisoned crossbows, pellet bows, lime poles, snare cords, nets and toils are all of it. Some sell them for silver and copper, some crave them for the belly's sake. Wherever the killing device is laid out, the flying birds lose their lives: necks snapped, the flock startled, breasts pierced and marrow run through. How bitter it is! The benevolent should redouble their compassionate hearts. Those who eat them — how can they bear to tie a grudge that must be repaid, in order to fill a dish that I might well do without? Those who make their living by it — why toil to create endless resentment and sin, to fill a purse that is limited?

A certain Dong loved to net flying birds. When he caught them, he would run a bamboo through their brains, singe their feathers with rice straw, and then sell them. Those he killed could not be counted. In old age he contracted a strange disease: over his whole body grew a coarse skin, scaly and wrinkled like a tree. When it itched, he would take rice straw and singe it. His head, too, ached, and he would have men beat it with bamboo. In the end he died of the disease. Again, Liu Dong'er made special use of crossbow bolts and destroyed a great many lives. One day he leaned at his door shooting at sparrows. It happened that his ear itched, and he used the point of the bolt to scratch the itching place. Suddenly the wind blew the door, which clapped against his hand, and the bolt went through his ear. Blood poured out like a stream, and he died. Alas! The crossbow shooting him, the straw singeing him — every one was as he himself had done. How cunning was the requital!

Wei Gao of the Tang kept a parrot. Whenever it heard the Buddha's name invoked, it would bow and bend and lean to receive it, and when it was made to invoke, it would loudly call Namo Amitabha Buddha. One day it passed away sitting upright and did not fall over; when it was burned, ten relics were found. Wei built a stupa and buried them. Again, in the Yuanyou era of the Song, a monk kept a mynah bird, which always followed the monk in invoking the Buddha. One day it lowered its head and folded its wings and passed away standing. The monk in charge pitied it and buried it. Suddenly on the burial place grew a single blue lotus, of a fragrance beyond the ordinary. When it was opened and looked at, the flower had grown out of the mynah's tongue root. The whole commandery came to see, and the governor made a verse, saying: Heaven brought forth a spiritual bird, the little eight-and-eight; it understood to follow the monk's mouth and invoke Amituo. A flying bird still realized the patience of non-arising — we who are men, how can we not equal it? Gathered together and seen thus, all the great and small kinds of creatures in the world belong to the living; our Buddha in his compassion protects them all equally and in every way. And men slaughter them — why?

Yan Maoyou of the Ming said: Men today all say that creation brings forth living things to nourish man and that it is only reasonable to chase and eat them. They do not know that man is himself one creature among Heaven and Earth. Only if he can cultivate the real and cherish life is he more spiritual than other creatures; otherwise, how is he different from the crawling things? Moreover, before a man has entered upon true cultivation, the wheel of rebirth among the destinies is not to be avoided. Those who are now of other kinds were perhaps human bodies in a former life; those who now have human bodies were perhaps of other kinds in a former life. Greed and anger, greed and killing, slay one another by borrowed hands. On the road of birth and death this is the most fearful thing. Once one enters the dark path, who knows that the one chased today may not become the chaser? Think of it, think of it.

Someone may say: If no man killed, then birds and beasts would fill the world; and as for jackals, wolves, tigers, and leopards, they would in turn eat men — would this not be to keep and raise creatures to harm men? I answer: The Buddha said that if a man has the merit of the compassionate heart, no weapon or army, no water or fire can harm him, and no evil beast or poisonous insect can injure him. Once there was a wicked king who drove fierce elephants, wishing to harm the Buddha. The Buddha roused his compassionate heart and his pity, and at the sight of the Buddha's five fingers, which turned into five lions roaring, the whole herd of elephants fell to the ground and submitted. Therefore the Nirvana Sutra praises the merit of the compassionate heart in this way. For at the utmost of compassion one can transform the utmost of violence in the world. In the time of Emperor Guangwu of the Han, the commandery of Hongnong had many tigers, and the governor ordered the people to set pit traps and take up bow and crossbow to deal with them, and the tiger trouble was all the worse. Then Liu Kun became governor, and said: This is what tyrannical government has brought about. He ordered the people each to fill in the pits and break their bows and crossbows, and to apply themselves only to carrying out benevolent government and pitying the hidden sorrows of the people, and the tigers thereupon crossed the river together and went away. Now Kun had never himself realized the great Way; with a single thought of benevolence he could at once subdue a violent tiger, how much more those who study the Buddha's compassion! And again, holy monks tame tigers and subdue dragons, clear before men's eyes and ears, and not to be denied. If all men could study the Buddha and study the holy monks, then even if tigers and leopards filled the world, they still could do no harm; what fear would there be of birds and beasts injuring men? For if cruel and violent men were all transformed into compassion, then poisonous and harmful creatures would all be transformed into unicorns and phoenixes. So we know that creatures, however fierce and venomous, still have in them something that can be moved and transformed; the only fear is that men cannot be compassionate.

The Cheng family of Dexing made their living by hunting with nets and arrows for generations, and the lives they killed could not be counted. One day they went into the market and bought several devil masks, and each of the grandsons put one on. Suddenly the dozens of hunting dogs they kept saw them and rushed forward to seize and bite, and could not be driven off, and all the grandsons were killed.

A man went into the mountains and brought home a baby monkey. The mother monkey followed him from behind all the way to his house. The man tied the baby monkey to a tree to show her, and the mother monkey beat her forehead and begged pitifully, only lacking the power of speech. The man would not let it go, and in the end struck and killed it. The mother monkey crouched down in grief and died. Within half a year an epidemic arose in that house and destroyed the whole family. Now the clever and the dull share one nature of awareness, and men and beasts both have father and son. Not only is the cause and effect of killing not to be escaped in a future life; even in the circumstances of the present, it is fearful before one's eyes. And do you people have no households of your own? Have you no parents, no wife and children? Suppose that he who governs the people should ruin your household by tyrannical government and maim your person by harsh punishment, so that your husband cannot keep his wife and your father cannot keep his son — would there be any who did not cry out to Heaven and weep, with a resentment too deep to dissolve?

When insects lie hidden in their dormancy, to disturb them must do them injury. Therefore the Most High wrote this to warn men, and all the buddhas above all cherish and pity them. How can a man fail to embody this meaning, and disturb them at random?

Cao Bin of the Song did not repair walls or houses in the depths of winter. When men asked him, the duke said: I fear harming the dormant insects. Cao's family were enfeoffed as kings for generations, and yet he would not disturb the dormant insects and plant a cause. Yet now there are those who burn off the wilds without cause, giving free play to a moment's sport and injuring ten thousand kinds of living creatures. Why do they not take Cao's affair and warn one another by it? If one meets with such a thing, one should at once beat it out. And as for the villagers and children who do this in their ignorance, one should all the more kindly instruct them. When households pour hot ashes or hot water on the ground, or burn paper money in sacrifice to the ancestors, they should in every case be mindful to preserve life as the place requires. No benevolence is greater.

When the birds have gone to roost it is as when men have gone to bed. If they are suddenly startled, will not the whole household be thrown into confusion? The Most High's warning has the same meaning as Confucius's not shooting at roosting birds. The Immortals' Scripture says: Whoever at any time finds means to save living creatures will surely obtain the recompense of blessing and long life.

Li Xizi was an old woman of the mountains. Whenever there was a great snow, and the birds had no branch to rest on, they would often gather at her house; the old woman would feed them with grain and did not dare startle them. The Most High said she had a benevolent heart, and she lived to five hundred years.

A certain Yang made his living catching birds. One day a winter magpie perched in a tree, and he set the lime and climbed the branch. The branch broke and he fell, and his brain was pierced by the bamboo, and he died with the blood flowing.

A burrow is the dwelling place where all living creatures gather. Seen from man's side, it is only a burrow; from theirs, it is their native ground and peaceful home, no different from man's. How can one fill it up, cutting off the gate of life and the way out, and bury the whole clan? How can one bear it?

Once there was a bhikshu who had obtained the six spiritual powers. He dwelt together with a novice monk, and in samadhi he saw that the novice would die within seven days. So he found an expedient and sent him home. After eight days the novice came back, and the bhikshu was astonished. Entering samadhi, he observed, and knew that the novice, on the road home, had seen an ant nest into which flood water was about to enter; he hastily took off his robe, fetched earth to dam the water, and kept it from entering. By this cause and condition his life was extended by twelve years. The novice thereby advanced diligently and attained the fourth fruit.

A certain commoner's wife of Hangzhou loved to kill living creatures, and above all hated ants, which soiled and spoiled her food and drink; she would straightway burn them to death. When she found an ant nest, she would either fill it up or scald it with hot water, and the ants she killed could not be counted. Afterward she bore a son. While he was still in arms, he was bitten all over by a swarm of ants, and his whole body swelled and rotted, and he died. Zhu Ji said: A woman's life is her son; to urge her to give up killing, one should show her this case, and she will know fear of herself. Therefore Ji's vow to give up killing contains the words: if I again raise the knife, I am killing my own sons and daughters. With one he warned himself, and with the other he warned the women of his house.

A nest is where all birds great and small rest and abide, suckle and give birth, and by which they avoid wind and rain, frost and snow, nets and arrows, and keep themselves sheltered. If the unkind overturn it, how is it different from wrecking a dwelling and burning a house? Does it not put them in a place of death? The Most High's Chapter on Preserving the Lineage says: When men's descendants dwindle and die out, it is in every case because in former lives they overturned nests and destroyed eggs, burned the mountains and drained the marshes, and caused abortions and miscarriages, and so transgressed the thousand six hundred and twenty articles of the statute. When one sees these words, those who have no descendants should the more sharply awake.

The Buddha said: If you see any man in the world climbing a tree to take eggs or going down into the water to take fish, you should silently invoke the Thus-Come One Supreme in Victory several tens of times, and they will be set free. This too is a method of saving life. Someone may say: Be kind to the people first, and then love the creatures; why does this teach only the loving of creatures? I answer: To be kind to the people is easy; to love creatures is hard. If one can bear to harm creatures, then one can surely bear to harm men. If one cannot bear to harm creatures, then what one is toward men may be known. Therefore the Avatamsaka Sutra says: I cannot bear even to do a painful thing to a single ant, how much less to a man. Tang of Shang extended the mind of removing the net so that it reached men, and so his benevolence covered all under Heaven. The King of Qi could not bear the trembling of a single ox, and to fill that out was enough to guard the four seas. If Bai Qi could have kept a heart that loves creatures, then the four hundred thousand at Changping need not have been buried alive. Therefore to love creatures and to love men are one benevolence. The Thus-Come One in his causal ground pitied a single dove, and extended it to the utmost, until compassion filled the ten directions and overflowed through a million kalpas. Who says that he who loves creatures cannot love men? If so, then thought after thought of saving the suffering is Avalokiteshvara appearing, and thought after thought of practicing compassion is Maitreya descending to be born.

Su Shi of the Song, courtesy name Zizhan, built a dwelling on the Eastern Slope and therefore called himself the Layman of the Eastern Slope. Before his study there were bamboos, cypresses, and all kinds of flowers, growing in thickets over the whole courtyard, and many birds made their nests in them. He forbade his children and servants to catch them, and within a few years they all nested in the low branches, so that their eggs could be looked down upon. I have heard of old that the feathered tribes will nest near men, wishing to be far from snakes, rats, owls, and kites. Now when men take their nestlings for meat and overturn their nests, are they not more unkind than the snakes and kites?

A little boy of the Xue family of Jizhou climbed a tree to search out a magpie's nest and take the nestlings. A large snake was there first, eating the nestlings in the nest. The boy first looked in alarm, and opened his mouth; the snake went into the boy's mouth. The boy fell into the water, and when they went to save him, the snake was eating the boy's heart, and boy and snake died together. Again, a certain Zhu of the Song loved to overturn nests, and especially hated bees; when he saw their hive, even high up, he would set up a ladder and destroy it. Afterward he had two sons, and both had their passages stopped up and died at once, and his line came to an end. Chan Master Cishou said: Men in the world mostly kill living creatures, and so there are the kalpas of weapon and army. Those whose lives you owe will kill your body; those whose wealth you owe will burn your house; they will scatter your wife and children. If you have broken another's nest and burrow, the echo is in each case like the sound. Wash your ears and hear what the Buddha says.

Yan Shaoting said: The sage's prohibition of killing was a matter of deep intent. The qilin is one beast among many, but because it does not tread on living grass nor eat living insects, men therefore make it auspicious and call it the chief of the four spiritual creatures. When a king has the virtue of benevolence, the qilin comes. It is also said: If you rip open the womb and kill the young, the qilin will not come to your suburbs; if you drain the marsh and dry up the fish, the dragon will not dwell in your pool; if you overturn nests and break eggs, the phoenix will not fly in your city. Thus did they show that a love of killing does not reach even to the birds and beasts. And do you say the sage did not prohibit killing? I have seen rascals who rob today and are bound tomorrow, and still rob without cease — because they think that in robbing they get gold and treasure at once, while the binding comes only tomorrow, and for the moment they have no leisure to consider it. Now to eat and drink is to please the mouth and belly at once, while the guilt lies far beyond the span of this body. No wonder that the doctrine of not killing grows ever more detailed and does not save men from slaughter. But let a man, at the moment when he holds the knife to catch and kill, try for a moment to turn his heart and look. Look at those living creatures: fleeing and flying and pouncing, casting themselves into the dark and into crevices, with no ladder to climb to heaven and no hole to bore into the earth — and compare them with us men when we fear the king's law and hear that there is a hunt and a pursuit, so that the soul flies and the spirit shakes: is there any difference or none? Look at those living creatures: their kind pity one another and perch and peck side by side. Cut one chicken and the whole flock cries out in alarm; slaughter one pig and the herd will not eat. Compare it with us men when we are seized and brought before the officials, and the whole household runs about in panic, or must part in death, and the six relations wail and weep, and the love of ordinary days is hard to cut and hard to let go: is there any difference or none? Look at those living creatures: bound and under the knife, writhing and wailing, hoping perhaps to be pardoned; the blood draining and the life cut off, the voice still angry and struggling, and at moments twitching. Compare it with us men when sickness leaves us helpless, crying to the gods and invoking the Buddha, hoping for protection; when the spirit-consciousness takes its leave, eyes staring and lips working, the hands rising and pulling, in the hope that it may yet live: is there any difference or none? Examine it closely and think it over. There is no need to speak of the fruit of a thousand births and ten thousand kalpas; even in the single thought of this present moment, dare one still bear to kill and wound?
